# Record 1

**Title:** The forgotten pectoralis minor syndrome: 100 operations for pectoralis minor syndrome alone or accompanied by neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome.

**Authors:** Sanders RJ, Rao NM

**Journal:** Annals of Vascular Surgery

**Year:** 2010

**Volume/Pages:** 24(6):701-8

**PMID:** 20471786

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.avsg.2010.02.022

**Abstract:** Since 2005 when researchers became aware of PMS, more than 75% of patients with NTOS also had neurogenic PMS, and approximately 30% had only NPMS without NTOS. Diagnosis relied on clinical assessment and muscle blocks with lidocaine. Pectoralis minor tenotomy was performed as an outpatient procedure. Among 76 patients receiving 100 operations (48 combined, 52 NPMS-alone), the PM-alone group demonstrated superior outcomes: "90% good-excellent, 2% fair, and 8% failed" compared to the combined group's 35% good-excellent and 46% failure rates. "All but one of the failures was immediate, only one was late." Recognition of PMS is clinically important since many suspected NTOS patients benefit from simple tenotomy, with thoracic outlet decompression available if needed.

---

# Record 2

**Title:** Pectoralis Minor Syndrome: Subclavicular Brachial Plexus Compression.

**Authors:** Sanders RJ, Annest SJ

**Journal:** Diagnostics (Basel)

**Year:** 2017

**Volume/Pages:** 7(3):46

**PMID:** 28788065

**DOI:** 10.3390/diagnostics7030046

**Abstract:** Diagnosis of brachial plexus compression (NTOS or NPMS) depends on "old fashioned history and physical examination." Scalene muscle and pectoralis minor muscle blocks confirm clinically suspected diagnoses. While electrodiagnostic studies can verify nerve compression, they cannot establish it. This represents positive diagnosis rather than exclusion diagnosis, with differential considerations addressed systematically. Conservative and surgical treatment options are reviewed.

# Research Records on Thoracic Outlet Syndrome

## Record 1
**Title:** The anterior scalene muscle in thoracic outlet compression syndrome. Histochemical and morphometric studies.

**Authors:** Machleder HI, Moll F, Verity MA

**Journal:** Arch Surg

**Year:** 1986

**Volume/Pages:** 121(10):1141-4

**PMID:** 3767646

**DOI:** 10.1001/archsurg.1986.01400100047009

**Abstract:** Histochemical studies and morphometric fiber type analysis were done on biopsy specimens of anterior scalene muscle (ASM) from patients with thoracic outlet compression syndrome (TOS), without structural abnormality. Hypertrophy and atrophy factors were determined from muscle fiber histograms of ASM from controls, patients with TOS, and after scalene tenotomy. Scalene muscle from patients with TOS showed marked type 1 (tonic contracting) fiber predominance "85.1% +/- 5.1%" and type 1 fiber hypertrophy "55.6 +/- 2.7 microns". After tenotomy there is a reduction of type 1 fiber representation, selective atrophy in the type 1 fiber system "atrophy factor, 0.66 +/- 0.24", and increase of type 2 fibers. These distinctive changes indicate that ASM is uniquely structured in fiber composition to sustain prolonged contraction. The ASM in patients with TOS demonstrates an extraordinary adaptive transformation and recruitment response in the type 1 fiber system reflecting chronic increased tone or motor neuron stimulation. These observations form a basis for clarifying the structural and pathophysiologic changes in TOS.

---

## Record 2
**Title:** Developmental anomalies at the thoracic outlet: an analysis of 200 consecutive cases.

**Authors:** Makhoul RG, Machleder HI

**Journal:** J Vasc Surg

**Year:** 1992

**Volume/Pages:** 16(4):534-42; discussion 542-5

**PMID:** 1404675

**DOI:** Not provided

**Abstract:** Anatomic observations were made during 200 consecutive transaxillary surgical procedures performed in 175 patients because of unremitting signs and symptoms of nerve or vascular compression at the thoracic outlet. There were 160 cases of brachial plexus compression and 40 cases of arterial or venous occlusion. "In 132 (66%) of these cases, single or multiple abnormalities were recognized" that represented developmental variations previously described in anatomic dissections or in embryologic studies. There were 17 cases of cervical rib or first thoracic rib abnormalities and 20 supernumerary scalene muscles. Developmental variations were identified in 86 scalene and 39 subclavius muscles or their insertions. Comparisons revealed a higher percentage of developmental anomalies in this group of patients than in consecutive anatomic investigations reported in unselected populations. This information was interpreted in light of recent embryologic studies and histochemical and morphometric ultrastructural studies of scalene muscle. The preponderance of evidence suggests that neurovascular compression in the region of the thoracic outlet derives from a combination of these factors: predisposing morphologic variations, structural modifications conditioned by functional requirements, and changes in fiber type or myosin isoform consequent to trauma. The correlation of clinical syndrome with morphologic characteristics alone was significant only for the Paget-Schroetter syndrome.

---

## Record 3
**Title:** Scalene muscle abnormalities in traumatic thoracic outlet syndrome.

**Authors:** Sanders RJ, Jackson CG, Banchero N, Pearce WH

**Journal:** Am J Surg

**Year:** 1990

**Volume/Pages:** 159(2):231-6

**PMID:** 2301718

**DOI:** 10.1016/s0002-9610(05)80269-7

**Abstract:** Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is not a single disorder but a collection of abnormalities in the same anatomic area that elicit similar symptoms. The many causes of TOS are best classified into one of three groups: osseous, traumatic, and nontraumatic. Although patients with traumatic TOS constituted "86%" of the last 600 patients with TOS who underwent surgical treatment, the precise mechanism underlying the condition remains obscure. To determine if there was microscopic abnormalities, 45 anterior and middle scalene muscles from patients with traumatic TOS were studied by means of histochemical stains applied after freezing of the muscles. The results revealed a consistent abnormal histologic pattern in patients with traumatic TOS: type II fibers were atrophied; there was an increase in the average number of type I fibers "78% versus 53% in muscles from control patients"; and there was a significant increase "mean: 36%" in connective tissue "muscles from control patients averaged less than 15%". Although type II fiber atrophy and type I fiber predominance are seen in a variety of other conditions, their association with fibrosis is rare. Following neck injuries, the changes in the anterior and middle scalene muscles are compatible with trauma, suggesting that fibrotic scalene muscles are an important cause of symptoms in traumatic TOS.

# Citation Summary

## Record 1
**Title:** The prevalence of cervical ribs in a London population.

**Authors:** Brewin J, Hill M, Ellis H

**Journal:** Clinical Anatomy

**Year:** 2009

**Volume/Pages:** 22(3):331-6

**PMID:** 19280652

**DOI:** 10.1002/ca.20774

**Abstract:** "Cervical ribs are an important cause of neurovascular compression at the thoracic outlet. Previous studies have shown the prevalence of cervical ribs to be between 0.05 and 3%, depending on the sex and race of the population studied. We examined 1,352 chest radiographs to determine the prevalence of cervical ribs in a London population of mixed sex and ethnicity. Our study found that the overall prevalence of cervical ribs was 0.74% with a higher rate in females compared with males (1.09 and 0.42%, respectively). Of the 10 individuals with a cervical rib, five were on the left, three were on the right and two were bilateral. The presence of elongated C7 transverse processes (transverse apophysomegaly) was also noted. We found a total of 30 elongated transverse processes with an overall prevalence of 2.21%. They were also more common in females (3.43%) than males (1.13%)."

---

## Record 2
**Title:** Comparison of three stretches for the pectoralis minor muscle.

**Authors:** Borstad JD, Ludewig PM

**Journal:** Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery

**Year:** 2006

**Volume/Pages:** 15(3):324-30

**PMID:** 16679233

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jse.2005.08.011

**Abstract:** "Pectoralis minor adaptive shortening in healthy individuals is associated with altered scapular kinematics similar to the alterations demonstrated in individuals with subacromial impingement. This associative relationship suggests that stretching of the pectoralis minor may improve scapular kinematics and assist in the management of shoulder impingement. Several stretches for the pectoralis minor are used clinically, although it is not known which stretch optimally lengthens the muscle. The purpose of this analysis was to compare the mean length change for 3 pectoralis minor stretches. Fifty subjects without shoulder pathology were examined for the change in length of the pectoralis minor during 3 separate stretches by use of an electromagnetic motion-capture system. The stretches analyzed were a unilateral self-stretch, a supine manual stretch, and a sitting manual stretch. Each stretch was significantly different from the other two (df, 2/98; F ratio, 39.09; P < .00001), with the unilateral self-stretch demonstrating the greatest length change (2.24 cm), followed by the supine manual stretch (1.69 cm) and the sitting manual stretch (0.77 cm). Knowledge of the most effective method of elongating the pectoralis minor muscle may improve clinical decision making when targeting this anterior scapulothoracic muscle as part of intervention for or prevention of shoulder impingement."

---

## Record 3
**Title:** The effect of long versus short pectoralis minor resting length on scapular kinematics in healthy individuals.

**Authors:** Borstad JD, Ludewig PM

**Journal:** Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy

**Year:** 2005

**Volume/Pages:** 35(4):227-38

**PMID:** 15901124

**DOI:** 10.2519/jospt.2005.35.4.227

**Abstract:** "STUDY DESIGN: Two-group comparison. OBJECTIVE: To compare scapular kinematics during arm elevation between groups distinguished by pectoralis minor resting length. BACKGROUND: Studies have demonstrated that individuals with subacromial impingement have altered scapular kinematics, such as loss of posterior tipping and increased internal rotation. One proposed mechanism for these alterations is an adaptively short pectoralis minor. This anterior scapulothoracic muscle may impact normal scapular kinematics if adaptively short. METHODS AND MEASURES: Fifty volunteers without shoulder pain were divided into long or short groups according to normalized pectoralis minor resting length. An electromagnetic motion capture system determined the angular orientation of the scapula, humerus, and trunk during arm elevation in 3 separate planes. Groups were compared for 3-dimensional scapular orientation relative to the trunk at arm elevation angles of 30 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees, and 120 degrees, using a mixed-model analysis of variance (ANOVA). RESULTS: There were statistically significant interaction effects between group and arm elevation angle for scapular tipping in all planes of arm elevation, with the scapula for the short group staying anteriorly tipped at higher angles. # Article 1

**Title:** Arm Numbness at 45 Degrees Abduction: A Case Report of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome After Brachial Neuritis

**Authors:** Fleet JL, Harish S, Bain J, Baker SK

**Journal:** J Rehabil Med Clin Commun

**Year:** 2020

**Volume/Pages:** 3:1000034

**PMID:** 33884136

**DOI:** 10.2340/20030711-1000034

**Abstract:** The case describes a 32-year-old woman with bilateral brachial neuritis who experienced "paraesthesias in her hand when abducting her shoulder to 45° or higher." Imaging revealed a kink in the superior trunk of the brachial plexus and narrowed costoclavicular space. Following unsuccessful conservative treatment, "partial anterior scalenectomy and neurolysis" improved symptoms, demonstrating how anatomical variations combined with post-brachial neuritis changes can produce thoracic outlet syndrome.

---

# Article 2

**Title:** Discovering Pathologies in the Anatomy Lab: The Case of Brachial Plexopathy Mimicking Neurological Thoracic Outlet Syndrome

**Authors:** Mancine R, Kowalski P, McMillan W, Geske N, Kujjo L

**Journal:** Spartan Med Res J

**Year:** 2020

**Volume/Pages:** 5(2):14179

**PMID:** 33655186

**DOI:** 10.51894/001c.14179

**Abstract:** During anatomy lab prosection, an "infero-lateral subclavicular lipoma" was discovered compressing the lateral cord and suprascapular nerve. The lipoma remained undiagnosed during the donor's life, being undetectable by CT imaging. The authors concluded physicians should consider atypical masses outside the thoracic outlet when standard treatments fail.

# Summary of Articles on Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Throwing Athletes

## 1. Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Overhead and Throwing Athletes

**Authors:** Troyer W, Gardner JE, Bowers RL

**Journal:** PM R (Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Journal)

**Year:** 2023

**Volume/Pages:** 15(5):629-639

**PMID:** 35403345

**DOI:** 10.1002/pmrj.12816

**Relevant Abstract Content:**
The authors note that "Throwing athletes are at increased risk of nTOS because of a variety of biomechanical factors." However, the full abstract does not provide specific mechanistic details about the throwing motion itself. Treatment typically involves surgical decompression through "muscle release, brachial plexus neurolysis, and first rib resection," with most athletes achieving symptom resolution and return to sport.

---

## 2. Nerve Compression Syndromes in Overhead Throwing Athletes

**Authors:** Zampeli F, Marín Fermín T, Hagert E

**Journal:** International Orthopaedics

**Year:** 2025

**Volume/Pages:** 49(4):827-834

**PMID:** 39960507

**DOI:** 10.1007/s00264-025-06453-z

**Relevant Abstract Content:**
This review highlights that "the overhead-throwing athlete may experience unique patterns of injuries" and identifies throwing as "a demanding manoeuvre that places a significant amount of stress across the upper limb." The article catalogs conditions including thoracic outlet syndrome but doesn't elaborate on specific biomechanical mechanisms in the provided abstract excerpt.

---

## 3. Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in High-Performance Athletes

**Authors:** Chandra V, Little C, Lee JT

**Journal:** Journal of Vascular Surgery

**Year:** 2014

**Volume/Pages:** 60(4):1012-7

**PMID:** 24835692

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jvs.2014.04.013

**Relevant Abstract Content:**
The authors note that "Repetitive upper extremity use in high-performance athletes is associated with the development" of TOS. Their study found 85% return to full competitive athletics, with nTOS patients showing improvement from mean QuickDASH scores of 40.4 preoperatively to 11.7 postoperatively.

# Summary of Articles on Weightlifting-Related Vascular and Thoracic Outlet Complications

---

## Article 1
**Title:** Paget-Schroetter Syndrome: A Case of a Young Weightlifter

**Authors:** Crossland DT, Overturf MD

**Journal:** Cureus

**Year:** 2024

**Volume/Pages:** 16(6):e62824

**PMID:** 39036114

**DOI:** 10.7759/cureus.62824

**Weightlifting Implicated:** Yes

**Mechanism:** Repetitive compression trauma during strenuous bench pressing caused subclavian vein compression and deep vein thrombosis. The space between the first rib and clavicle is vulnerable to "repetitive trauma due to extrinsic compression which ultimately results in scarring and clot formation."

---

## Article 2
**Title:** Underlying Subclavian Artery Occlusion Initially Misdiagnosed in Weightlifter Using Anabolic Steroids: A Case Report and Review of Literature

**Authors:** Meller L, Wilson K, Huang B, Kalavacherla S, Vitale K

**Journal:** Cureus

**Year:** 2023

**Volume/Pages:** 15(4):e37763

**PMID:** 37213978

**DOI:** 10.7759/cureus.37763

**Weightlifting Implicated:** Partially (comorbid factor)

**Mechanism:** While "anabolic steroid use is associated with arterial thrombosis," the case involved chronic subclavian artery occlusion in a weightlifter. The article suggests weightlifting combined with steroid use may contribute to thrombotic complications, though causality wasn't definitively established in this patient.

---

## Article 3
**Title:** Not All Gymnastic Exercises Are Suitable for Everyone: An Uncommon Cause of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: A Case Report

**Authors:** Wong DKH, Wong YW, Cheng SWK

**Journal:** JBJS Case Connect

**Year:** 2021

**Volume/Pages:** 11(2)

**PMID:** 33882031

**DOI:** 10.2106/JBJS.CC.20.00984

**Weightlifting Implicated:** Yes (secondary activity)

**Mechanism:** Patient involved in "rowing and weightlifting" with well-developed scalene muscles and narrowed costoclavicular spaces developed bilateral rib fracture-nonunions, causing thoracic outlet compression symptoms. The mechanism appears anatomically predisposed rather than directly traumatic.

---

## Article 4
**Title:** Weight Training Injuries: Part 2: Diagnosing and Managing Chronic Conditions

**Authors:** Reeves RK, Laskowski ER, Smith J

**Journal:** Phys Sportsmed

**Year:** 1998

**Volume/Pages:** 26(3):54-73

**PMID:** 20086792

**DOI:** 10.3810/psm.1998.03.811

**Weightlifting Implicated:** Yes

**Mechanism:** The repetitive nature and heavy loads of weight training contribute to thoracic outlet syndrome through nerve injuries. "Muscle hypertrophy, poor technique, or overuse can contribute to nerve injuries such as thoracic outlet syndrome."

# Research Summary: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Athletes

## Article 1
**Title:** Elasticity of the Scalene Muscles in Collegiate Baseball Pitchers Using Shear Wave Elastography

**Authors:** Takaba K, Takenaga T, Tsuchiya A, Takeuchi S, Fukuyoshi M, Nakagawa H, Futamura H, Futamura R, Sugimoto K, Murakami H, Yoshida M

**Journal:** Orthopedic Journal of Sports Medicine

**Year:** 2022

**Volume/Pages:** 10(8):23259671221114930

**PMID:** 36003968

**DOI:** 10.1177/23259671221114930

**Abstract (Verbatim):** "BACKGROUND: Thoracic outlet syndrome is more common in overhead athletes. The anterior and middle scalene muscles have been associated with thoracic outlet syndrome; however, the relationship between the elastic moduli of the scalene muscles and the overhead-throwing position has not been evaluated. PURPOSE: To investigate the elastic moduli of the anterior and middle scalene muscles in simulated throwing positions using shear wave elastography. STUDY DESIGN: Descriptive laboratory study. METHODS: We enrolled collegiate baseball players who underwent preseason medical checkups in January and February 2020. The anterior and middle scalene muscles were visualized in the short-axis view using ultrasound. In this view, the elastic moduli of the anterior and middle scalene muscles were measured using shear wave elastography in the following arm and neck positions: (1) adduction and neutral rotation of the shoulder (neutral), (2) 90° of abduction and external rotation of the shoulder (ABER), and (3) ABER with neck rotation toward the nonthrowing side (ABER+NR). Repeated-measures analysis of variance and a paired t test were used to compare the elastic modulus values among the 3 positions and between the 2 muscles, respectively. RESULTS: Overall, 30 baseball players were included. In both scalene muscles, the elastic moduli were significantly greater in the ABER versus neutral position (anterior scalene: 14.4 ± 3.8 vs 9.4 ± 2.0 kPa, respectively [P < .001]; middle scalene: 15.8 ± 5.0 vs 10.9 ± 3.4 kPa, respectively [P < .001]). In the neutral position, the elastic modulus was significantly greater in the middle scalene than the anterior scalene (10.9 ± 3.4 vs 9.4 ± 2.0 kPa, respectively; P = .03). In the ABER+NR position, the elastic modulus was significantly greater in the anterior scalene than the middle scalene (18.1 ± 4.6 vs 15.8 ± 2.6 kPa, respectively; P = .03). CONCLUSION: Because the ABER position was a simulation of the throwing position, these results indicate that this position could be associated with high elastic moduli of the scalene muscles, and both the anterior and middle scalene muscles may be involved."

---

## Article 2
**Title:** Thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes

**Authors:** Funakoshi T, Furushima K, Miyamoto A, Kusano H, Takahashi T, Inoue A, Shimokobe H

**Journal:** JSES International

**Year:** 2024

**Volume/Pages:** 8(3):620-629

**PMID:** 38707577

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jseint.2023.12.004

**Abstract (Verbatim):** "BACKGROUND: We aimed to retrospectively compare the clinical outcomes of endoscopy-assisted first-rib resection for thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) between overhead athletes and nonathletes and investigate the return to same-level sports rate in overhead athletes. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 181 cases with TOS (75 women, 106 men; mean age, 28.4 years; range, 12-57 years) who underwent endoscopy-assisted first-rib resection. We divided into two groups: 79 overhead athletes and 102 nonathletes groups. A transaxillary approach for first-rib resection and neurovascular decompression was performed under magnified visualization. Endoscopic findings related to the neurovascular bundle, interscalene distance, and scalene muscle were evaluated intraoperatively. We assessed the Roos and Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand scores, return to same-level sports rate, and ball velocity. RESULTS: Overhead athletes were significantly more likely to be men, younger, used the dominant side more frequently, and have a larger physique, more shoulder and elbow pain, and shorter symptom duration. The outcomes of the Roos score revealed significant differences in excellent or good results between overhead athletes (91.1%) and nonathletes (62.8%). The two groups significantly differed in preoperative and postoperative Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand and recovery rate scores (P = .007, < .001, < .001). CONCLUSION: Overhead athletes with TOS were more likely to be men, younger, dominant side more frequently, and have more shoulder and elbow pain, and a shorter symptom duration. Endoscopy-assisted transaxillary first-rib resection and neurolysis provided superior clinical outcomes in overhead athletes with TOS compared with nonathletes and a high return-to-same-level-play rate in sports."

---

## Article 3
**Title:** Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Sport: A Systematic Review

**Authors:** Garraud T, Pomares G, Daley P, Menu P, Dauty M, Fouasson-Chailloux A

**Journal:** Frontiers in Physiology

**Year:** 2022

**Volume/Pages:** 13:838014

**PMID:** 35755427

**DOI:** 10.3389/fphys.2022.838014

**Abstract (Verbatim):** "Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a rare and heterogeneous syndrome secondary to a compression of the neurovascular bundle in the thoracic outlet area. Muscle hypertrophy is recognized to induce vascular or neurogenic compression, especially in sports involving upper-arm solicitation. Athletes represent a distinctive population because of a specific management due to an ambitious objective, which is returning to high-level competition. We evaluated the scientific literature available for the management of TOS in athletes. Article research extended to March 2021 without other restriction concerning the date of articles publication. The search was performed independently by two assessors. A first preselection based on the article titles was produced, regarding their availability in English or French and a second preselection was produced after reading the abstracts. In case of doubt, a third assessor's advice was asked. Case reports were selected only if the sport involved was documented, as well as the level of practice. Cohorts were included if data about the number and the sport level of athletes were detailed. Seventy-eight articles were selected including 40 case reports, 10 clinical studies and 28 reviews of literature. Baseball pitchers seem to be highly at risk of developing a TOS. The surgical management appears particularly frequent in this specific population. The prognosis of TOS in athletes seems to be better than in the general population, possibly due to their better physical condition and their younger age. # Research Summary: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Athletes

## Article 1
**Title:** Elasticity of the Scalene Muscles in Collegiate Baseball Pitchers Using Shear Wave Elastography

**Authors:** Takaba K, Takenaga T, Tsuchiya A, Takeuchi S, Fukuyoshi M, Nakagawa H, Futamura H, Futamura R, Sugimoto K, Murakami H, Yoshida M

**Journal:** Orthopedic Journal of Sports Medicine

**Year:** 2022

**Volume/Pages:** 10(8):23259671221114930

**PMID:** 36003968

**DOI:** 10.1177/23259671221114930

**Abstract (Verbatim):** "BACKGROUND: Thoracic outlet syndrome is more common in overhead athletes. The anterior and middle scalene muscles have been associated with thoracic outlet syndrome; however, the relationship between the elastic moduli of the scalene muscles and the overhead-throwing position has not been evaluated. PURPOSE: To investigate the elastic moduli of the anterior and middle scalene muscles in simulated throwing positions using shear wave elastography. STUDY DESIGN: Descriptive laboratory study. METHODS: We enrolled collegiate baseball players who underwent preseason medical checkups in January and February 2020. The anterior and middle scalene muscles were visualized in the short-axis view using ultrasound. In this view, the elastic moduli of the anterior and middle scalene muscles were measured using shear wave elastography in the following arm and neck positions: (1) adduction and neutral rotation of the shoulder (neutral), (2) 90° of abduction and external rotation of the shoulder (ABER), and (3) ABER with neck rotation toward the nonthrowing side (ABER+NR). Repeated-measures analysis of variance and a paired t test were used to compare the elastic modulus values among the 3 positions and between the 2 muscles, respectively. RESULTS: Overall, 30 baseball players were included. In both scalene muscles, the elastic moduli were significantly greater in the ABER versus neutral position (anterior scalene: 14.4 ± 3.8 vs 9.4 ± 2.0 kPa, respectively [P < .001]; middle scalene: 15.8 ± 5.0 vs 10.9 ± 3.4 kPa, respectively [P < .001]). In the neutral position, the elastic modulus was significantly greater in the middle scalene than the anterior scalene (10.9 ± 3.4 vs 9.4 ± 2.0 kPa, respectively; P = .03). In the ABER+NR position, the elastic modulus was significantly greater in the anterior scalene than the middle scalene (18.1 ± 4.6 vs 15.8 ± 2.6 kPa, respectively; P = .03). CONCLUSION: Because the ABER position was a simulation of the throwing position, these results indicate that this position could be associated with high elastic moduli of the scalene muscles, and both the anterior and middle scalene muscles may be involved."

---

## Article 2
**Title:** Thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes

**Authors:** Funakoshi T, Furushima K, Miyamoto A, Kusano H, Takahashi T, Inoue A, Shimokobe H

**Journal:** JSES International

**Year:** 2024

**Volume/Pages:** 8(3):620-629

**PMID:** 38707577

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jseint.2023.12.004

**Abstract (Verbatim):** "BACKGROUND: We aimed to retrospectively compare the clinical outcomes of endoscopy-assisted first-rib resection for thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) between overhead athletes and nonathletes and investigate the return to same-level sports rate in overhead athletes. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 181 cases with TOS (75 women, 106 men; mean age, 28.4 years; range, 12-57 years) who underwent endoscopy-assisted first-rib resection. We divided into two groups: 79 overhead athletes and 102 nonathletes groups. A transaxillary approach for first-rib resection and neurovascular decompression was performed under magnified visualization. Endoscopic findings related to the neurovascular bundle, interscalene distance, and scalene muscle were evaluated intraoperatively. We assessed the Roos and Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand scores, return to same-level sports rate, and ball velocity. RESULTS: Overhead athletes were significantly more likely to be men, younger, used the dominant side more frequently, and have a larger physique, more shoulder and elbow pain, and shorter symptom duration. The outcomes of the Roos score revealed significant differences in excellent or good results between overhead athletes (91.1%) and nonathletes (62.8%). The two groups significantly differed in preoperative and postoperative Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand and recovery rate scores (P = .007, < .001, < .001). CONCLUSION: Overhead athletes with TOS were more likely to be men, younger, dominant side more frequently, and have more shoulder and elbow pain, and a shorter symptom duration. Endoscopy-assisted transaxillary first-rib resection and neurolysis provided superior clinical outcomes in overhead athletes with TOS compared with nonathletes and a high return-to-same-level-play rate in sports."

---

## Article 3
**Title:** Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Sport: A Systematic Review

**Authors:** Garraud T, Pomares G, Daley P, Menu P, Dauty M, Fouasson-Chailloux A

**Journal:** Frontiers in Physiology

**Year:** 2022

**Volume/Pages:** 13:838014

**PMID:** 35755427

**DOI:** 10.3389/fphys.2022.838014

**Abstract (Verbatim):** "Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a rare and heterogeneous syndrome secondary to a compression of the neurovascular bundle in the thoracic outlet area. Muscle hypertrophy is recognized to induce vascular or neurogenic compression, especially in sports involving upper-arm solicitation. Athletes represent a distinctive population because of a specific management due to an ambitious objective, which is returning to high-level competition. We evaluated the scientific literature available for the management of TOS in athletes. Article research extended to March 2021 without other restriction concerning the date of articles publication. The search was performed independently by two assessors. A first preselection based on the article titles was produced, regarding their availability in English or French and a second preselection was produced after reading the abstracts. In case of doubt, a third assessor's advice was asked. Case reports were selected only if the sport involved was documented, as well as the level of practice. Cohorts were included if data about the number and the sport level of athletes were detailed. Seventy-eight articles were selected including 40 case reports, 10 clinical studies and 28 reviews of literature. Baseball pitchers seem to be highly at risk of developing a TOS. The surgical management appears particularly frequent in this specific population. The prognosis of TOS in athletes seems to be better than in the general population, possibly due to their better physical condition and their younger age. Some studies showed interesting and encouraging results concerning return to previous sport level. Literature shows a strong link between TOS and certain sports. Unfortunately, this syndrome still lacks rigorous diagnostic criteria and management guidelines for athletes."

# Summary of Three Pectoralis Minor Studies

**Study 1**
- **Title:** "Resting position variables at the shoulder: evidence to support a posture-impairment association"
- **Author:** Borstad JD
- **Journal:** Physical Therapy
- **Year/Volume/Pages:** 2006;86(4):549-57
- **PMID:** 16579671
- **DOI:** Not provided in content

The research examined 50 asymptomatic subjects divided by pectoralis minor resting length. Key findings showed "significant group differences...for thoracic spine kyphosis and scapular internal rotation," with the sternal notch-to-coracoid distance showing strongest correlation to muscle length.

---

**Study 2**
- **Title:** "Measurement of pectoralis minor muscle length: validation and clinical application"
- **Author:** Borstad JD
- **Journal:** Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
- **Year/Volume/Pages:** 2008;38(4):169-74
- **PMID:** 18434665
- **DOI:** 10.2519/jospt.2008.2723

This validation study used electromagnetic motion capture on cadavers and clinical instruments in vivo, demonstrating "high intraclass correlation coefficients" between measurement techniques using palpable landmarks.

---

**Study 3**
- **Title:** "Reliability of measuring pectoralis minor muscle resting length in subjects with and without signs of shoulder impingement"
- **Authors:** Rosa DP, Borstad JD, Pires ED, Camargo PR
- **Journal:** Brazilian Journal of Physical Therapy
- **Year/Volume/Pages:** 2016;20(2):176-83
- **PMID:** 26982455
- **DOI:** 10.1590/bjpt-rbf.2014.0146

With 100 participants, reliability testing showed ICC values of "0.86-0.97" for intrarater and "0.95 for between-day reliability," using flexible tape measure measurement standing.

**Title:** Positional compression of the axillary artery causing upper extremity thrombosis and embolism in the elite overhead throwing athlete

**Authors:** Duwayri YM, Emery VB, Driskill MR, Earley JA, Wright RW, Paletta GA Jr, Thompson RW

**Journal:** J Vasc Surg

**Year:** 2011

**Volume/Pages:** 53(5):1329-40

**PMID:** 21276687

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jvs.2010.11.031

**Abstract:**
"Repetitive positional compression of the axillary artery can cause a spectrum of pathology in the overhead athlete, including focal intimal hyperplasia, aneurysm formation, segmental dissection, and branch vessel aneurysms. Prompt recognition of these rare lesions is crucial given their propensity toward thrombosis and distal embolism, with positional arteriography necessary for diagnosis. Full functional recovery can usually be anticipated within several months of surgical treatment, consisting of mobilization and segmental reconstruction of the diseased axillary artery or ligation/excision of branch aneurysms, as well as concomitant management of distal thromboembolism."

**Title:** Thoracic Outlet Syndrome from Bilateral Cervical Ribs -A Clinical Case Report

**Authors:** Cu N, Ec I, Rt E, Cv O

**Journal:** J Orthop Case Rep

**Year:** 2018

**Volume/Pages:** 8(2):78-80

**PMID:** 30167420

**DOI:** 10.13107/jocr.2250-0685.1060

**Abstract:** "Cervical rib is a mesenchymal or cartilaginous elongation of the transverse process of usually the seventh, rarely the sixth, and very rarely the fifth cervical vertebrae." The case describes a 28-year-old female soldier presenting with 3 years of neck and right shoulder pain with radiating symptoms. Imaging revealed bilateral cervical ribs with brachial plexus compression and cervical cord syrinx formation. Right cervical rib excision provided complete symptom resolution; left rib excision 8 months later similarly resolved remaining symptoms by 12-month follow-up.

**Volume/Pages:** 48(5):710-5

**PMID:** 23952042

**DOI:** 10.4085/1062-6050-48.5.03

**Abstract:** A 23-year-old collegiate wrestler sustained a neck injury during competition, experiencing "pain, weakness, and numbness in his left upper extremity." Initial imaging and conservative treatment were unsuccessful. MRI revealed T1-T2 disc herniation compressing a postfixed brachial plexus, a rare anatomic variant. Surgical intervention was required to enable the athlete's return to competition.

**Title:** Subclavian vein obstruction and thoracic outlet syndrome: a review of etiology and management

**Authors:** Sanders RJ, Haug C

**Journal:** Annals of Vascular Surgery

**Year:** 1990

**Volume/Pages:** 4(4):397-410

**PMID:** 2141997

**DOI:** 10.1007/BF02000508

**Abstract:**

This is a comprehensive review of acute and chronic venous obstruction, both thrombotic and nonthrombotic. It covers the anatomy, etiology, clinical features, management, and results of treatment of this uncommon condition. "The typical clinical symptoms are pain and swelling in the arm, aggravated by exercise." Venography serves as the essential diagnostic test. Treatment outcomes for acute thrombosis included: anticoagulants showing 49% improvement in 185 cases; fibrinolysis demonstrating 74% improvement in 62 cases (36 subsequently underwent first rib resection, 3 had angioplasty); and thrombectomy achieving 94% improvement in 33 cases. For chronic obstruction: first rib resection yielded 77% improvement in 97 patients; claviculectomy showed 83% improvement in six patients; scalenectomy and soft tissue division achieved 83% improvement in 23 cases; endovenectomy demonstrated 90% improvement in 10 cases; and venous bypass produced 67% improvement in 15 cases. "The definitions of 'improvement' are variable and sometimes ambiguous." The data support individualized treatment approaches rather than rigid guidelines.

**Title:** Defining Diagnostic Criteria for Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: An Expert Consensus

**Authors:** Wagner ER, Sullivan CM, Cuneo KR, Chopra KN, Omole O, Gottschalk MB, Bowers RL

**Journal:** Orthopedic Journal of Sports Medicine

**Year:** 2026

**Volume/Pages:** 14(5):23259671261440925

**PMID:** 42169800

**DOI:** 10.1177/23259671261440925

**FULL ABSTRACT:**

"BACKGROUND: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS) can present itself in a number of ways, often resulting in diagnostic ambiguity. PURPOSE: To establish a consensus among upper extremity experts using the Delphi method to determine the most clinically relevant criteria in distinguishing nTOS to help create a diagnostic algorithm. STUDY DESIGN: Consensus statement. METHODS: A panel of 20 upper extremity experts rated the importance of 54 different clinical items in reference to distinguishing nTOS. Items were ranked on a scale from 0 (least important) to 10 (most important). The mean and standard deviation for each item's rankings were calculated. The Cronbach alpha (α) value was used to determine the degree of concordance among the panelists' rankings. Analogous items with similarly high rankings were combined to help develop the final criteria. RESULTS: A Cronbach α value of .936 was calculated, indicating a high degree of consensus among the experts' responses. Similar items with higher rankings were combined to help develop the final criteria. The 5 criteria deemed clinically important for nTOS were (1) a positive response to injections (pectoralis minor, anterior scalene, middle scalene); (2) upper or lower trunk radiating symptoms that worsen with supraclavicular provocative maneuvers (scalene pressure or positive Tinel sign over scalenes); (3) upper or lower trunk symptoms that worsen with infraclavicular provocative maneuvers (positive Tinel sign medial to coracoid or tenderness to palpation over the coracoid process); (4) reproduction of pain with 90° of abduction in external rotation or upper limb tension test, and (5) participation in work/exercise requiring repetitive arm stress (overhead athletes, throwing sports, protracted posture at work, etc). CONCLUSION: This study proposed 5 clinical criteria for distinguishing nTOS that were agreed upon by 20 upper extremity, nerve, and vascular surgery experts. These criteria can be used to develop a future diagnostic algorithm for nTOS, allowing for further research and more efficient nTOS treatment."

PURPOSE: To establish a consensus among upper extremity experts using the Delphi method to determine the most clinically relevant criteria in distinguishing nTOS to help create a diagnostic algorithm. STUDY DESIGN: Consensus statement. METHODS: A panel of 20 upper extremity experts rated the importance of 54 different clinical items in reference to distinguishing nTOS. Items were ranked on a scale from 0 (least important) to 10 (most important). The mean and standard deviation for each item's rankings were calculated. The Cronbach alpha (α) value was used to determine the degree of concordance among the panelists' rankings. Analogous items with similarly high rankings were combined to help develop the final criteria. RESULTS: A Cronbach α value of .936 was calculated, indicating a high degree of consensus among the experts' responses. Similar items with higher rankings were combined to help develop the final criteria. The 5 criteria deemed clinically important for nTOS were (1) a positive response to injections (pectoralis minor, anterior scalene, middle scalene); (2) upper or lower trunk radiating symptoms that worsen with supraclavicular provocative maneuvers (scalene pressure or positive Tinel sign over scalenes); (3) upper or lower trunk symptoms that worsen with infraclavicular provocative maneuvers (positive Tinel sign medial to coracoid or tenderness to palpation over the coracoid process); (4) reproduction of pain with 90° of abduction in external rotation or upper limb tension test, and (5) participation in work/exercise requiring repetitive arm stress (overhead athletes, throwing sports, protracted posture at work, etc). CONCLUSION: This study proposed 5 clinical criteria for distinguishing nTOS that were agreed upon by 20 upper extremity, nerve, and vascular surgery experts. These criteria can be used to develop a future diagnostic algorithm for nTOS, allowing for further research and more efficient nTOS treatment."

**Title:** The thoracic outlet syndromes: Part 2. The arterial, venous, neurovascular, and disputed thoracic outlet syndromes.

**Volume/Pages:** 56(4):663-673

**PMID:** 28006856

**Abstract:** "The thoracic outlet syndromes (TOSs) are a group of etiologically and clinically distinct disorders with 1 feature in common: compression of 1 or more neurovascular elements as they traverse the thoracic outlet." # Citation Information

**Title:** Innovative Dynamic Ultrasound Diagnosis of First Rib Stress Fracture in an Adolescent Athlete-A Case Report

**Authors:** Yoon Y, Lam KHS, Park C, Lee J, Kye J, Kim H, Kim S, Kang J, Suhaimi A, Suryadi T, Su DC, Reeves KD, Cavallino S

**Journal:** Diagnostics (Basel)

**Year:** 2025

**Volume/Pages:** 15(19):2437

**PMID:** 41095656

**DOI:** 10.3390/diagnostics15192437

---

## Abstract

First rib stress fractures prove exceptionally uncommon in young athletes and typically go unrecognized due to overlapping symptoms with scapular dyskinesis. This case describes a 12-year-old elite pitcher presenting with progressive scapular winging and audible snapping during throwing. Imaging demonstrated cortical disruption at the serratus anterior attachment point rather than the typical costotransverse location. "High-resolution musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSK-US) identified cortical disruption with periosteal edema, and dynamic ultrasound reproduced the patient's snapping and pain in real time." Conservative rehabilitation spanning three phases—scapular stabilization, serratus activation, and structured return-to-throwing—achieved complete healing and pain-free sport resumption within 12 weeks. The findings emphasize MSK-US advantages for detecting such fractures in adolescents and demonstrate how dynamic examination reveals functional pathophysiology beyond static anatomy.

# TOS Risk Factors: Key Findings

## (a) Congenital Bands/Ligaments - Roos Classification
Roos identified **14 types** of fibromuscular anomalies. The document states: "He noted the presence of many fibrous and muscular accessory fibers in the area, which he classified into 14 types."

## (b) Cervical Rib Prevalence in General Population
The prevalence is reported as **1.1%**: "The incidence of cervical ribs is estimated to be 1.1% in the general population (the vast majority of them remain asymptomatic)"

## (c) Symptomatic Cervical Rib Cases
The document does not explicitly state what percentage of people with cervical ribs become symptomatic. However, it notes cervical ribs occur in 29.5% of TOS patients versus 1.1% in the general population, indicating most remain asymptomatic, but no specific symptomatic percentage is provided.

## (d) Three Key Anatomical Spaces

**Interscalene triangle:** "created anteriorly by the anterior scalene (AS), posteriorly by the middle scalene (MS), and inferiorly by FR" containing "the trunks of the BP and anteriorly located to it, the subclavian artery"

**Costoclavicular space:** Superior boundary is the clavicle; through it pass "BP divisions and a subclavian artery"

**Subcoracoid/pectoralis minor space:** "The superior limit is the coracoid process of the scapula, to which the pectoralis minor muscle attaches" with contents including "cords, axillary artery, and axillary vein"

## (e) Scalene Muscle Anomalies and Frequency
In one study of 200 TOS patients: "20 cases were associated with the supernumerary scalene muscle. There were 86 cases with scalene developmental variation"

Imaging studies identified compression of the axillary vein caused by enlarged pectoralis minor muscle, diagnosed as McCleery syndrome—"a rare entity within the multiple thoracic outlet syndrome aetiologies." # Citation Information

**Title:** Neurovascular compression syndrome of the upper thoracic outlet

**Authors:** Tsuladze II, Usachev DY, Dreval ON, Magomedov RK, Kuznetsov AV, Vakatov DV, Kozlova YA, Chapandze GN, Kuldashev KA, Mukhina OV

**Journal:** Zh Vopr Neirokhir Im N N Burdenko

**Year:** 2025

**Volume/Pages:** 89(6):106-112

**PMID:** 41307980

**DOI:** 10.17116/neiro202589061106

---

## Full Abstract

"Neurovascular compression syndrome of the upper thoracic outlet is a collective term encompassing various entities: cervical ribs, structural variations of the first rib, costoclavicular syndrome, fibromuscular anomalies of anterior and middle scalene muscles, pectoralis minor syndrome and various pathologies of subclavian vessels."

The authors trace the historical development of understanding these conditions from Galen's description of cervical ribs through modern approaches. Key milestones include Bramwell's identification of first rib variations (1903), Todd's work on costoclavicular narrowing (1912), and recognition of scalene muscle involvement (1929). The authors conclude that consolidating these disparate entities under one diagnostic classification—neurovascular compression syndrome—better reflects the shared mechanism of vascular-nerve bundle compression within the cervicoaxillary canal.

I have a solid verified corpus. Before finalizing, here are the load-bearing claims I intend to make, so they can be checked:

1. **Roos band count**: primaries say **seven** (Am J Surg 1976) and **nine** (Acta Chir Belg 1980). The widely-cited "14 types" appears only in a 2023 secondary review (Maślanka, J Clin Med) — I could not verify a Roos primary describing 14. I'll report all three and flag the discrepancy.
2. **Swift & Nichols 1984** describes a *traction* mechanism (symptoms worse with downward traction, relieved by arm elevation; T2 visible above the shoulders on lateral C-spine film), not explicitly costoclavicular narrowing as the task framed it.
3. **Borstad/Ludewig pec minor work was done in healthy non-athletes**, not overhead athletes — the athlete link is inference.
4. **GIRD ↔ TOS returns zero PubMed records**. No evidence.
5. **No cohort or controlled evidence that resistance training causes TOS** — only case reports.

# AbstractText Content

Here is the AbstractText element reproduced verbatim:

"Careful anatomic studies during 1,120 operations for thoracic outlet syndrome indicate that most TOS patients have anomalous fibromuscular bands near the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels that predispose them to neurovascular symptoms in the shoulder and upper extremity. Nine different types of these "soft tissue" anomalies not visible on roentgenograms have been identified during these operations. The anomalies often are multiple, and may or may not be associated with bone abnormalities as well. These anomalies are clearly associated with the symptoms of thoracic outlet syndrome, particularly the neurologic type, as they apparently irritate or compress the brachial plexus. Thus, it finally becomes clear why the majority of symptoms of TOS are neurologic in nature, rather than vascular, and why the positional pulse tests and arteriograms, strongly advocated in the past for this diagnosis, have proved generally unreliable. Furthermore, the anomalous bands explain why the electromyogram and nerve conduction tests are of little benefit in establishing the accurate diagnosis of TOS. They even indicate the most reliable clinical tests to establish the diagnosis, and dictate the most appropriate surgical procedures required to offer permanent relief. If patients with shoulder, arm and hand symptoms are carefully evaluated with appropriate tests, and then highly selected for surgical treatment after conservative measures fail, gratifying relief may still be obtained in over 90% of patients with severe thoracic outlet syndrome, providing the diagnosis is correct, and the proper operation is performed with great care."

**Exact number word used:** "Nine"

# Thoracic Outlet Imaging Studies

## Study 1
**Title:** "Ultrasonographic assessment of arterial cross-sectional area in the thoracic outlet on postural maneuvers measured with power Doppler ultrasonography in both asymptomatic and symptomatic populations"

**Authors:** Demondion X, Vidal C, Herbinet P, Gautier C, Duquesnoy B, Cotten A

**Journal:** J Ultrasound Med

**Year:** 2006

**Volume/Pages:** 25(2):217-24

**PMID:** 16439785

**DOI:** 10.7863/jum.2006.25.2.217

**Abstract:** "The purpose of this study was to evaluate the feasibility and potential usefulness of power Doppler ultrasonography (PDU) in the assessment of changes in arterial cross-sectional area in the thoracic outlet during upper limb elevation. Forty-four volunteers and 28 patients with a clinical diagnosis of arterial thoracic outlet syndrome were evaluated by B-mode imaging and PDU. Arterial cross-sectional area was assessed in the 3 compartments of the thoracic outlet with the arm alongside the body and at 90 degrees, 130 degrees, and 170 degrees of abduction. The percentage of arterial stenosis was calculated for each of these arm positions. Nineteen of the 28 patients were also assessed by magnetic resonance (MR) imaging. No significant arterial stenosis was shown in the interscalene triangle and in the retropectoralis minor space of the volunteers and patients. A significant difference (P < .01) in stenosis between volunteers and patients was seen for all degrees of abduction in the costoclavicular space. The 130 degrees hyperabduction maneuver appeared to be the most discriminating postural maneuver. Seven patients assessed with MR imaging did not have any arterial stenosis on MR images, whereas an appreciable degree of arterial stenosis was shown with ultrasonography. Arterial compression inside the thoracic outlet can be detected and quantified with B-mode imaging in association with PDU."

**Measurements:** No specific numerical measurements of compartment dimensions provided.

---

## Study 2
**Title:** "Thoracic outlet: assessment with MR imaging in asymptomatic and symptomatic populations"

**Authors:** Demondion X, Bacqueville E, Paul C, Duquesnoy B, Hachulla E, Cotten A

**Journal:** Radiology

**Year:** 2003

**Volume/Pages:** 227(2):461-8

**PMID:** 12637678

**DOI:** 10.1148/radiol.2272012111

**Abstract:** "To compare the dynamic modifications of the thoracic outlet in asymptomatic volunteers and symptomatic patients and assess the presence and location of vasculonervous compressions in these two populations. Thirty-five healthy volunteers and 54 patients with clinical symptoms of thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) underwent magnetic resonance (MR) imaging of the thoracic outlets with their arms alongside their bodies and after a postural maneuver. Measurements were obtained at the interscalene triangle (thickness of anterior scalene muscle, interscalene angle), at the costoclavicular space (minimum costoclavicular distance, distance between inferior border of subclavius muscle and the anterior chest wall, maximum thickness of subclavius muscle, angle between first rib shaft and horizontal), and at the retropectoralis minor space (distance between posterior border of pectoralis minor muscle and posterior lining of axilla at the passage of the axillary vessels, thickness of pectoralis minor muscle). The presence and location of vasculonervous compressions were also assessed. Patients with TOS had a smaller costoclavicular distance after the postural maneuver (P <.001), a thicker subclavius muscle in both arm positions (P <.001), and a wider retropectoralis minor space after the postural maneuver (P <.001) than did volunteers. Venous compressions after the postural maneuver were observed in 47% of volunteers and 63% of patients at the prescalene space, in 54% of volunteers and 61% of patients at the costoclavicular space, and in 27% of volunteers and 30% of patients at the retropectoralis minor space. Arterial and nervous compressions, respectively, were seen in 72% and 7% of patients. No arterial or nervous compression was seen in volunteers. Except for venous thrombosis, vasculonervous compressions were demonstrated only with arm elevation. Only three thoracic outlet measurements differed significantly in both populations. MR imaging appeared helpful in demonstrating the location and cause of arterial or nervous compressions."

**Measurements:** No absolute numerical measurements reported; only statistical comparisons (P-values) between groups.

---

## Study 3
**Title:** "Thoracic outlet: anatomic correlation with MR imaging"

**Authors:** Demondion X, Boutry N, Drizenko A, Paul C, Francke JP, Cotten A

**Journal:** AJR Am J Roentgenol

**Year:** 2000

**Volume/Pages:** 175(2):417-22

**PMID:** 10915686

**DOI:** 10.2214/ajr.175.2.1750417

**Abstract:** "The purpose of this report is to describe the normal MR anatomy of the thoracic outlet and its modification after postural maneuvers using an anatomic-MR imaging correlation. MR imaging appears to be a useful technique to study the thoracic outlet and its contents because of its excellent soft-tissue depiction and its multiplanar capabilities. T1-weighted images obtained in the sagittal plane clearly depicted the different compartments of the cervicothoracic-brachial junction. Hyperabduction maneuvers may have potential applications in the assessment of the thoracic outlet syndrome by showing the location of compression."

**Measurements:** No specific numerical measurements provided.

# TOS in Overhead Throwing Athletes — Anatomical, Postural & Biomechanical Causes

**Scope:** mechanism only. Where a cited paper is a treatment series, I extracted only its anatomic/mechanistic finding and deliberately left its outcome data out (noted inline).

**Verification method:** PubMed's HTML interface is cookie-walled to WebFetch. Every citation below was verified through the NCBI E-utilities API (`efetch.fcgi`, `db=pubmed`), which returns the authoritative MEDLINE record — title, authors, journal, year, volume/pages, DOI, abstract. Nothing below rests on a WebSearch summary.

---

## VERIFIED CITATIONS

### Congenital / structural
1. **Roos DB.** Congenital anomalies associated with thoracic outlet syndrome. Anatomy, symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment. *Am J Surg* 1976;132(6):771-8. PMID 998867. DOI 10.1016/0002-9610(76)90456-6. — Describes **seven** fibromuscular band types; one third of 58 cadaver outlets had ≥1 of them.
2. **Roos DB.** Pathophysiology of congenital anomalies in thoracic outlet syndrome. *Acta Chir Belg* 1980;79(5):353-61. PMID 7223264. — Verbatim: *"Nine different types of these 'soft tissue' anomalies not visible on roentgenograms have been identified"* across 1,120 operations.
3. **Makhoul RG, Machleder HI.** Developmental anomalies at the thoracic outlet: an analysis of 200 consecutive cases. *J Vasc Surg* 1992;16(4):534-42. PMID 1404675. — 66% had developmental abnormalities; 20 supernumerary scalenes; 86 scalene and 39 subclavius variations.
4. **Brewin J, Hill M, Ellis H.** The prevalence of cervical ribs in a London population. *Clin Anat* 2009;22(3):331-6. PMID 19280652. DOI 10.1002/ca.20774. — Cervical rib 0.74%; elongated C7 transverse process 2.21%.
5. **Ezeofor SN, Njeze NR, Aghaji MN, Onuh AC, Obikili EN.** The prevalence of cervical ribs in Enugu, Nigeria. *Niger J Clin Pract* 2016;19(4):513-6. PMID 27251970. DOI 10.4103/1119-3077.183315. — 0.7% of 6,571 radiographs.
6. **Harry WG, Bennett JD, Guha SC.** Scalene muscles and the brachial plexus: anatomical variations and their clinical significance. *Clin Anat* 1997;10(4):250-2. PMID 9213042. — Textbook plexus-between-scalenes arrangement in only 60% of 51 cadavers.
7. **Maślanka K, Zielinska N, Karauda P, Balcerzak A, Georgiev G, Borowski A, Drobniewski M, Olewnik Ł.** Congenital, Acquired, and Trauma-Related Risk Factors for Thoracic Outlet Syndrome — Review of the Literature. *J Clin Med* 2023;12(21):6811. PMID 37959276. DOI 10.3390/jcm12216811. — Secondary source; defines the three spaces; states cervical rib 1.1% general vs 29.5% of TOS patients; attributes **14** band types to Roos (see COULD NOT VERIFY).
8. **Krishnan KG, Mucha D, Gupta R, Schackert G.** Brachial plexus compression caused by recurrent clavicular nonunion and space-occupying pseudoarthrosis. *Neurosurgery* 2008;62(5 Suppl 2):ONS461-9. PMID 18596530. DOI 10.1227/01.neu.0000326036.54714.17. — Clavicular nonunion callus as a space-occupying plexus compressor.
9. **Coris EE, Higgins HW 2nd.** First rib stress fractures in throwing athletes. *Am J Sports Med* 2005;33(9):1400-4. PMID 16002484. DOI 10.1177/0363546505275349. — **Existence verified via MEDLINE record + MeSH (Baseball/injuries; Fractures, Stress; Biomechanical Phenomena). No abstract exists in PubMed; I assert no findings from it.**
10. **Funakoshi T, Furushima K, Kusano H, Itoh Y, Miyamoto A, Horiuchi Y, Sugawara M, Itoh Y.** First-Rib Stress Fracture in Overhead Throwing Athletes. *J Bone Joint Surg Am* 2019;101(10):896-903. PMID 31094981. DOI 10.2106/JBJS.18.01375. — 24 fractures, mean age 16.8 y, dominant arm; *"some patients may have symptoms consistent with thoracic outlet syndrome."*
11. **Suehara Y, et al.** Arterial Thoracic Outlet Syndrome and Cerebellar Infarction Following a Stress Fracture of the First Rib and Extensive Callus Formation. *JBJS Case Connect* 2017;7(3):e64. PMID 29252893. DOI 10.2106/JBJS.CC.17.00001. — Baseball player; callus → arterial TOS.
12. **Yoon Y, Lam KHS, et al.** Innovative Dynamic Ultrasound Diagnosis of First Rib Stress Fracture in an Adolescent Athlete. *Diagnostics (Basel)* 2025;15(19):2437. PMID 41095656. DOI 10.3390/diagnostics15192437. — 12-y-old elite pitcher; fracture at the **serratus anterior** attachment, not the usual costotransverse site.

### Scalene pathology
13. **Machleder HI, Moll F, Verity MA.** The anterior scalene muscle in thoracic outlet compression syndrome. Histochemical and morphometric studies. *Arch Surg* 1986;121(10):1141-4. PMID 3767646. ## KEY FINDINGS

### 1. The three compression spaces — and which one actually matters in throwers

**ESTABLISHED (anatomy).** Boundaries and contents, per Maślanka 2023 / Illig 2016 / Ferrante 2017:
- **Interscalene triangle** — anterior scalene anteriorly, middle scalene posteriorly, first rib inferiorly. Contains the **brachial plexus trunks** and the **subclavian artery**. The subclavian *vein* passes anterior to the anterior scalene, so it is not in this triangle.
- **Costoclavicular space** — clavicle/subclavius above, first rib below. Contains plexus **divisions**, subclavian artery **and** vein.
- **Subcoracoid / retropectoralis minor space** — pectoralis minor and its coracoid insertion anteriorly, chest wall posteriorly. Contains plexus **cords**, axillary artery and vein.

**ESTABLISHED (positional behaviour — Demondion 2006, PDU, 44 volunteers + 28 arterial-TOS patients, arm at 0/90/130/170°):** *"No significant arterial stenosis was shown in the interscalene triangle and in the retropectoralis minor space of the volunteers and patients. A significant difference (P<.01) in stenosis between volunteers and patients was seen for all degrees of abduction in the costoclavicular space. The 130 degrees hyperabduction maneuver appeared to be the most discriminating."* For **arterial** compression, the costoclavicular space is the discriminating site — not the subcoracoid space.

**PLAUSIBLE BUT UNPROVEN — "subcoracoid space is most implicated in throwers."** The reasoning chain that supports it is: (a) Sanders & Rao 2010 found >75% of nTOS patients also had neurogenic pectoralis minor syndrome and ~30% had PMS *alone* — but that is a **general surgical TOS population, not athletes**; (b) Wagner 2026 expert consensus lists infraclavicular provocative findings (Tinel medial to coracoid, coracoid tenderness) among the 5 nTOS criteria — expert opinion, not measurement; (c) Bottros 2017 applied pec minor blocks specifically in high-performance overhead athletes — **but that record has no abstract in PubMed, so I assert nothing from it.** No study I could verify compares the three spaces head-to-head in throwers. **Report this as a clinically favoured hypothesis, not a fact.**

### 2. Congenital / structural predisposition

**ESTABLISHED.**
- **Roos band types: seven in 1976, nine in 1980.** Roos 1976 (Am J Surg): seven fibromuscular band types, and *"One third of fifty-eight cadaver thoracic outlets dissected showed at least one of the seven muscular anomalies recognized at operations."* Roos 1980 (Acta Chir Belg), verbatim from 1,120 operations: *"Nine different types of these 'soft tissue' anomalies not visible on roentgenograms have been identified during these operations. The anomalies often are multiple, and may or may not be associated with bone abnormalities as well."* **Use nine, cite Roos 1980.** The commonly repeated "14 types" is not supported by any Roos primary I could find (see COULD NOT VERIFY).
- **Cervical rib prevalence: 0.74%** overall in 1,352 London chest radiographs (Brewin 2009) — **females 1.09%, males 0.42%**; independently corroborated at **0.7%** in 6,571 Nigerian radiographs (females 1.1%, males 0.2%; Ezeofor 2016). Brewin notes prior studies span 0.05–3% by sex and race.
- **Elongated C7 transverse process is ~3× commoner than a cervical rib: 2.21%** overall (females 3.43%, males 1.13%; Brewin 2009). This is the more likely bony contributor in any given athlete.
- **Scalene anatomy is highly variable.** Harry 1997: in 51 cadavers, the textbook arrangement of the plexus passing between anterior and middle scalene *"was found in only 60% of instances."*
- **Structural anomalies are common in TOS surgical series.** Makhoul & Machleder 1992, 200 consecutive transaxillary procedures: *"In 132 (66%) of these cases, single or multiple abnormalities were recognized"* — 17 cervical/first-rib abnormalities, 20 supernumerary scalene muscles, 86 scalene and 39 subclavius developmental variations.
- **Clavicle malunion/nonunion can compress the plexus** — Krishnan 2008, eight cases of space-occupying clavicular pseudarthrosis producing brachial plexus compression.
- **First rib stress fracture occurs in throwers and can produce TOS.** Funakoshi 2019 (JBJS): 24 first-rib stress fractures, mean age 16.8 y, dominant arm, posterior shoulder pain on throwing; *"some patients may have symptoms consistent with thoracic outlet syndrome."* Suehara 2017: callus after a first-rib stress fracture in a baseball player caused arterial TOS with cerebellar infarction. Yoon 2025: a 12-y-old elite pitcher's fracture was at the **serratus anterior attachment**, presenting as scapular winging and snapping — i.e. the fracture can masquerade as a scapular-control problem.

**IMPORTANT CAVEAT — do not overstate "not the coach's fault."** The same literature that establishes predisposition also establishes that predisposition ≠ causation. Roos found his anomalies in one third of *asymptomatic cadaver* outlets. Makhoul & Machleder concluded: *"The correlation of clinical syndrome with morphologic characteristics alone was significant only for the Paget-Schroetter syndrome"* — i.e. for everything except effort thrombosis, anatomy alone did not predict the clinical picture; they attributed TOS to *"predisposing morphologic variations, structural modifications conditioned by functional requirements, and changes in fiber type or myosin isoform consequent to trauma."* The honest framing is **structural anomalies are common, usually silent, and become symptomatic when loaded** — which makes them a screening and load-management issue rather than an exoneration.

### 3. Scalene muscle pathology

**ESTABLISHED — Machleder, Moll & Verity 1986 (Arch Surg), anterior scalene biopsies in TOS patients without structural abnormality:**
- Type 1 (tonic/slow) fiber predominance **85.1% ± 5.1%**
- Type 1 fiber hypertrophy **55.6 ± 2.7 µm**
- After scalene tenotomy: reduced type 1 representation, selective type 1 atrophy (atrophy factor **0.66 ± 0.24**), increased type 2 fibers
- Authors' interpretation, verbatim: the anterior scalene *"demonstrates an extraordinary adaptive transformation and recruitment response in the type 1 fiber system reflecting chronic increased tone or motor neuron stimulation."*

**ESTABLISHED — Sanders, Jackson, Banchero & Pearce 1990 (Am J Surg), 45 anterior and middle scalene muscles in traumatic TOS:**
- Type II fibers **atrophied**
- Type I fibers **78% vs 53% in controls**
- Connective tissue **mean 36%, vs <15% in controls** — a significant increase
- Verbatim: *"Although type II fiber atrophy and type I fiber predominance are seen in a variety of other conditions, their association with fibrosis is rare. Following neck injuries, the changes in the anterior and middle scalene muscles are compatible with trauma, suggesting that fibrotic scalene muscles are an important cause of symptoms in traumatic TOS."*
- Traumatic TOS accounted for **86%** of their last 600 surgical TOS patients.

**ESTABLISHED — neck trauma as the dominant acquired trigger.** Sanders, Hammond & Rao 2007 (J Vasc Surg): nTOS arises from *"brachial plexus compression usually from scarred scalene muscles secondary to neck trauma, whiplash injuries being the most common."* Note this is stated as the authors' clinical position; the 2007 paper has no structured abstract and gives no denominator.

**The two histology studies agree on direction but differ on magnitude** (85% vs 78% type I). Both are surgical-biopsy series without randomisation; controls are convenience samples. Treat the *pattern* (type I predominance + type II atrophy + fibrosis) as established, the *exact percentages* as study-specific.

### 4. Posture and scapular position

**ESTABLISHED, with a mechanism correction — droopy shoulder syndrome.** Swift & Nichols 1984 (*Neurology* 34:212-5) describe *"low-set, 'droopy' shoulders and long swan neck,"* with the radiographic sign that on a lateral cervical film the **T2 vertebra is visible above the shoulders**. Critically, symptoms **worsened with downward traction and improved when patients elevated their arms**, predominantly in women, with no abnormal vascular or neurologic findings but a Tinel's sign over the plexus. **This pattern is brachial plexus traction/stretch, not compression of a narrowed costoclavicular space** — relief on arm *elevation* is the opposite of what costoclavicular compression predicts. If the brief frames droopy shoulder as costoclavicular narrowing, that is a misattribution; report it as a **traction** mechanism. (Clein 1976 described the same entity earlier in *CMAJ*, also emphasising the radiographic sign and the absence of neurologic findings.)

**ESTABLISHED — pectoralis minor shortness alters scapular kinematics, in healthy adults.** Borstad & Ludewig 2005 (JOSPT), 50 asymptomatic volunteers split by normalised pec minor resting length, electromagnetic motion capture during elevation in 3 planes: the short group's scapula **stayed anteriorly tipped at higher elevation angles** (significant group × angle interaction in all planes) and was **more internally rotated** at lower coronal-plane angles. Borstad 2006 (*Phys Ther*), same cohort design: significant group differences for **thoracic kyphosis and scapular internal rotation**, with sternal-notch-to-coracoid distance correlating most strongly with muscle length.

**ESTABLISHED — measurement.** Borstad 2008 (JOSPT) validated clinical measurement of pec minor length against electromagnetic motion capture in cadavers and in vivo using palpable landmarks (coracoid to the 4th rib/sternocostal junction), reporting high ICCs. Rosa 2016 (*Braz J Phys Ther*, n=100) found intrarater ICC **0.86–0.97** and between-day ICC **0.95** with a flexible tape in standing. **I could not verify any specific "pectoralis minor index" cut-off value from these abstracts — report the method, not a threshold.**

**IMPORTANT SCOPE CAVEAT.** All of the Borstad/Ludewig work above was done in **healthy, asymptomatic, non-athlete adults**, and its stated clinical target was **subacromial impingement**, not TOS. Extending it to overhead throwers, and from impingement to subcoracoid neurovascular compression, is a two-step inference. It is a reasonable one, but it is **plausible-unproven**, not established.

**PLAUSIBLE — the scapular route to subcoracoid narrowing.** Ahmed 2023 (pathoanatomy section): *"The combination of repetitive overhead activity and scapular dyskinesia leads to contracture... creating a chronically distalized and protracted scapular posture."* This is a narrative pathoanatomy statement in a surgical-technique paper, not a measurement study.

### 5. Throwing-specific biomechanics

**ESTABLISHED — the ABER (throwing) position stiffens both scalenes.** Takaba 2022 (*OJSM*), 30 collegiate baseball pitchers, shear wave elastography, verbatim:
- Anterior scalene: **14.4 ± 3.8 kPa in ABER vs 9.4 ± 2.0 kPa neutral** (P<.001)
- Middle scalene: **15.8 ± 5.0 vs 10.9 ± 3.4 kPa** (P<.001)
- Neutral: middle > anterior (10.9 vs 9.4 kPa, P=.03)
- **ABER + neck rotation to the non-throwing side: anterior > middle (18.1 ± 4.6 vs 15.8 ± 2.6 kPa, P=.03)** — i.e. adding contralateral neck rotation flips which scalene is stiffer and drives anterior scalene stiffness to roughly double its neutral value.
- Authors' conclusion: *"this position could be associated with high elastic moduli of the scalene muscles, and both the anterior and middle scalene muscles may be involved."*
This is the cleanest mechanistic link between the cocking position and interscalene-triangle loading. It measures **muscle stiffness**, not nerve compression.

**ESTABLISHED — positional narrowing is real, but is also normal.** Demondion 2003 (*Radiology*), 35 asymptomatic volunteers and 54 TOS patients, MR in neutral and after a postural manoeuvre. Measurements taken at all three spaces (anterior scalene thickness, interscalene angle; minimum costoclavicular distance, subclavius thickness, first-rib angle; retropectoralis minor distance, pec minor thickness). TOS patients had:
- **smaller costoclavicular distance after the postural manoeuvre (P<.001)**
- **thicker subclavius in both arm positions (P<.001)**
- **wider retropectoralis minor space after the manoeuvre (P<.001)** ← counterintuitive; worth stating plainly
- Venous compression after the manoeuvre in **47% of volunteers vs 63% of patients** (prescalene), **54% vs 61%** (costoclavicular), **27% vs 30%** (retropectoralis minor)
- Arterial compression **72% of patients, 0% of volunteers**; nerve compression **7% of patients, 0% of volunteers**
- *"Except for venous thrombosis, vasculonervous compressions were demonstrated only with arm elevation."*
- *"Only three thoracic outlet measurements differed significantly in both populations."*

**Two things the brief should take from Demondion 2003:** (a) compression is a **positional phenomenon** — it does not exist at rest; (b) **roughly half of asymptomatic people show positional venous compression**, so a positive provocative finding in a thrower is weak evidence on its own. Only arterial and nerve compression discriminated.

**ESTABLISHED — arterial pathology in elite throwers is a recognised entity.** Duwayri 2011 (*J Vasc Surg*, Thompson's group): *"Repetitive positional compression of the axillary artery can cause a spectrum of pathology in the overhead athlete, including focal intimal hyperplasia, aneurysm formation, segmental dissection, and branch vessel aneurysms,"* requiring **positional arteriography** for diagnosis. This is **arterial**, distinct from nTOS.

**ESTABLISHED — demographic profile of the affected thrower.** Funakoshi 2024 (JSES Int, 181 TOS cases, 79 overhead athletes vs 102 non-athletes): athletes were significantly more likely to be **male, younger, dominant-side, of larger physique**, with more shoulder and elbow pain and shorter symptom duration. (Their outcome data is out of scope and excluded here.)

**PLAUSIBLE BUT UNPROVEN — cumulative narrowing from repeated hyperabduction/ER.** The chain — ABER stiffens scalenes (Takaba), compression appears only with elevation (Demondion), repetition produces scalene fibrosis (Sanders 1990, in trauma patients) — is coherent, but no longitudinal study measures cumulative outlet narrowing across a throwing season. Narrative reviews assert it (Troyer 2023: *"Throwing athletes are at increased risk of nTOS because of a variety of biomechanical factors"*; Zampeli 2025) without primary data.

**NO EVIDENCE — GIRD.** PubMed returns **zero** records for `"glenohumeral internal rotation deficit"[tiab] AND "thoracic outlet"[tiab]`, **zero** for `GIRD[tiab] AND "thoracic outlet"[tiab]`, and **zero** for `"internal rotation deficit"[tiab] AND "thoracic outlet"[tiab]`. Any GIRD→TOS link in the brief is **speculation**. Scapular dyskinesis fares only slightly better: 7 records, of which the substantive one is a narrative pathoanatomy statement (Ahmed 2023).

**Cervical spine contribution — thin.** Upton & McComas 1973 (*Lancet*) established the double-crush concept and is verified to exist, but has no PubMed abstract, so I assert nothing from it. Ferrante & Ferrante 2017 Parts 1 and 2 (*Muscle Nerve*) are the authoritative modern treatment of the differential, including cervical radiculopathy, and Part 2 argues that "disputed TOS" should be recategorised as **cervicoscapular pain syndrome**. **No study quantifying cervical foraminal narrowing as a contributor to nTOS in throwers was found.** Treat cervical contribution as an established differential-diagnosis concern and an unquantified mechanistic hypothesis.

### 6. Does heavy resistance training cause TOS?

**Honest answer: there is no controlled or cohort evidence that resistance training causes TOS. None.** A targeted PubMed search — `"thoracic outlet syndrome"[tiab] AND (weightlifter OR weightlifting OR bodybuilder OR bodybuilding OR powerlifter OR "weight training" OR "resistance training")[tiab]` — returned **12 records total**, of which most were irrelevant (StatPearls, physician epidemiology, blood-flow-restriction safety). What exists is:

**Case reports only (level 4/5 evidence):**
- **Crossland 2024** (Cureus): Paget-Schroetter (venous, effort thrombosis) in a young weightlifter, attributed to repetitive compression during **bench pressing** in the costoclavicular space.
- **Wong 2021** (JBJS Case Connect): a **rowing + weightlifting** athlete with well-developed scalenes and narrowed costoclavicular spaces, bilateral rib fracture-nonunions.
- **Meller 2023** (Cureus): chronic subclavian artery occlusion in a weightlifter — **confounded by anabolic steroid use**, and the authors did not establish causality.
- **Ligh 2009** (CORR): a Division I pitcher with *"intermittent axillary artery compression with the arm in abduction resulting from **hypertrophy of the pectoralis minor and scalene muscles**."* This is the closest thing to direct support for the hypertrophy mechanism — but the hypertrophy is attributed to throwing, not to a documented lifting programme.
- **Starčević 2024** (J Clin Med): McCleery syndrome (positional axillary vein compression) from **pectoralis minor hypertrophy** in a water polo player.

**Narrative assertions without primary data:**
- Garraud 2022 systematic review: *"Muscle hypertrophy is recognized to induce vascular or neurogenic compression, especially in sports involving upper-arm solicitation."* The review located 78 articles — **40 case reports, 10 clinical studies, 28 reviews** — and concluded the field *"still lacks rigorous diagnostic criteria and management guidelines for athletes."* That composition is itself the finding: the evidence base is case reports.
- Reeves 1998 (*Phys Sportsmed*): *"Muscle hypertrophy, poor technique, or overuse can contribute to nerve injuries such as thoracic outlet syndrome."* Expert opinion, 1998, no supporting data.

**Specifically searched and NOT found:** any study associating heavy pressing without pec minor length work, heavy overhead pressing, or shrug/upper-trap loading with TOS. No such paper exists in PubMed that I could locate.

**How to state this in the brief:** The claim "lifting causes TOS" is **unsupported**. The defensible statement is narrower — *pectoralis minor and scalene hypertrophy have been documented as the compressing structure in individual athlete case reports, and the sports implicated are throwing, water polo, rowing and weightlifting; whether training-induced hypertrophy raises TOS risk at a population level has never been tested.* Note also the direction-of-causation problem: Machleder 1986 and Sanders 1990 show the scalene changes in TOS are **fibrosis plus type I predominance with type II atrophy** — that is a chronic-tone/injury signature, **not the type II hypertrophy signature of resistance training**. That histological mismatch is a genuine argument against the "lifting built the compressing muscle" story, and is worth making explicitly.
